# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Eleanor and I both want to try a pair in our own real setting before buying, and Ruth and Walter both want it to keep up with lots of voices at once, so each pair belongs together and both names are plain; Diego's point that it costs too much fits neither group, so leaving it on its own is right.
whys.g2: Tomás's answer about sitting on his good side doesn't say what would make it worth more, so it is off-topic, and it was rightly kept out of the groups.

founder.order_why: Screen 14 (who else has to agree) belongs next to screens 10 and 11 (who decides). Instead it comes after the cost and price screens (12 and 13), so the buyer question is split by the money questions.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14 both ask whether anyone besides the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides or has to agree. Screens 15 and 16 then check and choose the same buyer and payer alignment a third time. Screens 3 and 4 also carry the identical context question.
founder.missing: The price screen has no way to say one-off hardware plus an optional subscription ($599 glasses, free captions, $20/month Pro). It also gives no place to say the glasses are HSA/FSA eligible, which changes who effectively pays. Nothing asks what they rely on today (hearing aids, phone caption apps, lipreading). And nothing checks that they keep a phone with them, paired and online, which the glasses need to work.

PRIMARY.order_why: The study jumps from asking what AirCaps is worth straight to a follow-up and then to step 4 of 5, so step 3 seems to be missing, and I was asked to price it before anyone asked what I use now.
PRIMARY.missing: What I do today when a conversation with hearing people goes too fast or gets too noisy, such as lip-reading, asking people to repeat, a captioning app on my phone, my hearing aids or bringing someone along, and how well that works. Also, the missed-conversations question asks about last month, but nothing asks about the last week, even though the first screen is about talking with hearing people every week.

screens.why1: After who decides, what it costs and the price, asking what first step I'd want a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult to take is the obvious next question on whether they'll pay.
screens.why2: 'What's the first real step you'd want them to take?' is plain to me, and the hint's time, data, money or a signature tells me what counts.
screens.why3: I know my own funnel: someone orders a pair of glasses and has 15 days to send them back, so I can answer this straight away.
screens.why4: A free-text box with one escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', fits a founder who isn't sure, and nothing is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair with free returns' keeps my words, including 'free returns', and adds no 'now', timing or number I didn't type.
screens.why7: The step is on the card's one measure, the belief can be supported or refuted by yes/probably yes against probably not/no, and the chip is the founder's allowed 'I'm not sure'; but the hint allows 25 words where the card caps the step at 9, and because ordering a pair costs money the card wants a smaller no-cost step, which this screen never asks for.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take? (up to 9 words, e.g. 'order a pair of glasses with free returns'). If it costs them money: what smaller free step would come first? (e.g. 'the free captions on their phone')

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, it makes sense for Keel to show it back as strangers will hear it, with the belief it will test, before I move on.
screens.why2: "Order a pair with free returns" and the one-in-three bar read cleanly to me on first pass.
screens.why3: It is my own step, and checking it is squarely my job; I know we ship with 15-day risk-free returns.
screens.why4: The one row is my step, under nine words, with the belief and bar beside it, and nothing odd or missing on the row itself.
screens.why5: It is word for word what I typed, "order a pair with free returns", with no added *now*, timing or number, and the belief keeps it intact.
screens.why7: The measure and belief hold and *free returns* is kept, but two rules bend: "a pair" never names what it acts on (glasses), and ordering costs $599 up front yet no free smaller step is listed, so the soft yes falls back to a bare *Probably yes*.
screens.instead: Step: order a pair of AirCaps glasses with free returns; smaller step: free live captions on your phone first. Belief: Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair of AirCaps glasses with free returns.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step (order a pair with free returns), asking whether to collect people who would actually try it, before the study goes out, is the obvious next move.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' with the hint spelling out the exact line respondents see and where I find the yeses is plain to me as a YC founder, even though 'pilot' leans B2B for a consumer glasses product.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of deaf and hard-of-hearing people ready to try the glasses is my own call and I can answer it at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape is needed.
screens.why5: The line strangers will see, 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.', drops the step I just typed, order a pair with free returns, so the ask they meet is softer and vaguer than my real commitment.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you order a pair with 15-day free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my questions belongs right before the link goes out to strangers.
screens.why2: Daphne, Saskia, the 5-second samples and the 400 credits are all plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I can pick a voice, but most of my respondents are deaf or hard of hearing and will read the captions, so judging which voice suits them is partly a guess.
screens.why4: Two voices are distinct, but for a deaf audience the option I most want, a captions-first or text-only interviewer with no voice, is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps my people as deaf or hard-of-hearing adults and leaks nothing of AirCaps into the interviewer choice.
screens.instead: How should Keel ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Captions first with Daphne's voice / Captions first with Saskia's voice / Text only, no voice

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it is obvious I now pick how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents take the interview.
screens.why2: Every option is in plain words, and for my audience the line that Daphne's questions are also written on screen answers my first worry.
screens.why3: I know my users and how they communicate, so I can choose the format from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover voice-led, text-only and the respondent's own choice, and the read-and-tap one I picked is the natural fit for people who rely on text.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my respondents as deaf or hard-of-hearing adults and does not alter anything I typed.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how they answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Each option is in plain words I'd use myself (my own contacts, a list from Keel's search, one link posted in a group), and 'Contacts page' names Keel's own page.
screens.why3: I know who I'd reach: hard-of-hearing people I've met through TranscribeGlass by name, or one open link posted in groups like HLAA chapters or deaf and hard-of-hearing Facebook groups.
screens.why4: The three ways to reach people are distinct and cover how I'd actually find wearers, and a choice of channel needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name each with their own link, is shown as I chose it, and nothing about AirCaps is changed.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the deciding number, 1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month, and the tally shows 2 of 5 beliefs not holding.
screens.why_b2: Each card says what is counted, over 7 people, and where my bar sits (5 of 7), though the numbering jumping from 4 to 6 made me look twice for a missing card.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are my words, but my cost estimate was $200 to $1,500 a year and here it is 12 lost conversations a month, and my $599 to $839 a year is restated as $599 up front then $20 a month.
screens.why_b4: 'Smaller than you think' and 'below your price' tell me which way I am wrong, but nothing says what to change, such as a lower price, the free plan as the entry, or which segment loses more.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, but the screen never says 7 is a small sample, and lines like 'they lose less today than you estimated' speak for all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults from seven answers.
screens.instead: Not holding up on money: of 7 people, none valued it at $599 and only 1 loses a dozen conversations a month, yet 6 of 7 would order with free returns, so test a lower entry price or the free plan with a bigger group before relaunching.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits beside the deciding count, 1 of 7 at or above my low against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 cells, 1 for and 6 against, but the unit line stutters ('conversations of the conversations they are in a month') and the marker sits at 5 on a 0 to 15 axis where I said 12, so I had to look twice to see the 5 is people, not conversations.
screens.why_b3: The dimension name is mine, but I typed Existing sacrifice as money, $200 to $1,500 a year spent on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, and this belief is a count of about 12 conversations a month that I never typed.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and points me to the Price card, but it doesn't say what this means for my price against what they spend today, or whether to drop my estimate.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and 'a lean, not a call' are on the screen, but 'they lose less today than you estimated' compares people against an estimate I never made, and 'miss' could mean skipping a conversation as well as losing its thread, so the 'less than you think' reading is softer than the headline says.
screens.instead: Keep my money: 'You said $200 to $1,500 a year', ask 'Last year, about how much did you spend on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras?' in dollars a year, and say what that spend means for a $599 pair.

screens.why_b1: The verdict (Not holding up) sits right beside the numbers that decide it: 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front, 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each.
screens.why_b2: Each chart labels every band with its count and for or against, marks my $599 and my $20 as a band's low edge, and draws the bar at 5 of 7, so the result reads at a glance.
screens.why_b3: Price is my dimension and $599 is my number, but 'then $20 a month' turns my optional Pro plan into a required fee (I offer a free plan with unlimited captions), so the belief and the against-on-either rule are not quite what I sell.
screens.why_b4: The So line shows where people landed ($250 to under $599, 6 of 7), but it stops at pointing me to the Insights tab and never says what this means for my price, such as testing a lower up-front price or a trial pair, even though four quotes ask to try a pair first.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen flags it as 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than seven people said; the soft 'fewer than 2 in 3' only understates a 0 of 7.
screens.instead: None of 7 would pay $599 up front: six put it at $250 to under $599, and several want to try a pair in their own noisy setting first. Test a price under $599, or a loaner or demo, and treat the $20 Pro plan as optional rather than counting it against you.

screens.why_b1: Not reached is stated with the deciding number right beside it, 0 of 7 named my price or more, so I know this card decides nothing and why.
screens.why_b2: The bars all read 0 and the strip is five ghost cells with no marker, so I have to look again to see that the chart counts nobody and that five is the floor, not a bar it was measured against.
screens.why_b3: The belief is Keel's derived line, not one I checked on the way in, and the card does not say Keel wrote it; it is recognisable from my $599 and $20 a month.
screens.why_b4: The So line says the card waits until 5 reach the price, which is true but generic; it does not point me back to Price as the thing to fix first, either the price or who I ask.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the 7: it says nobody was asked, gives each person's band, and calls nothing held or failed.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 named $599 up front or more (most said $250 to $599), so nobody was asked where the money would come from. Fix Price first, then this card can be read.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 decided alone against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts last-purchase answers over 7 people, with one bar each for and against, and the marker at 5 makes the bar plain at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Buyer and payer and carries word for word the belief I checked: the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else must agree first.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count (they decide alone; 1 of 7 needed agreement) and doesn't tell me what that means for selling AirCaps, such as pitching the wearer directly with no spouse or family step to plan for.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the count line says outright that this is a small group, a lean and not a call, so nothing overclaims.
screens.instead: So: sell straight to the wearer, since only 1 of 7 (Walter) needed a spouse's say; who signs isn't your problem, the price is.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers to my ordering question over 7 people, and the strip puts my bar at 5 with 6 for and 1 against, so all three are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title Commitment and the belief 'Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair with free returns' are exactly what I checked, and the yes option uses my own step.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is a push to act, but it is vague about what booking a pair order means (take the order? send the link?) and it does not say this is a yes to a returnable order with no price on it, so I don't know whether to put the $599 in front of these six next.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the So line then treats it as a call ('Book them into it'), a soft overstatement for 6 of 7 on a question that named free returns and no price.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would order a pair with free returns, a lean from 7 people: ask these six to order at $599 with the 15-day return and see who actually does.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Not holding up' with '0 of 7 at $599 or more, once · then: 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month · bar 5 of 7 on each' right beside it, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b3: Price, and the belief that deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would think AirCaps worth $599 up front then $20 a month, are the price I set and the line I checked on the Price card.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what this means for AirCaps; the groups hint at a trial and multi-speaker pickup, but no line tells me what to change, such as leading with the 15-day returns I already offer or testing a lower entry price.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n plain (7 against, 6 asked here, Amaka never saw it), each group is only 2 people with no claim of strength, and every quote carries the person's own price brackets.
screens.why_b6: I learn things I never typed: people want to try a pair in their own setting before buying even though returns are free; the real test is crowd and audience voices, not one speaker; one-sided hearing loss is managed by seating; most would pay $250 to under $599 and under $10 a month.
screens.instead: Add a line under the box: 'Most would pay $250 to $599 and under $10 a month; four of six want proof in their own noisy room first -- your 15-day free returns isn't reaching them, so say it up front, then test a lower entry price or a cheaper monthly plan.'

screens.why1: As the first question it makes sense to check that I actually deal with hearing people week to week before asking anything else.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is exactly how I and everyone I know say it, and the question is short and single.
screens.why3: I know without guessing; I'm with hearing people at work, in shops and at the doctor's every week.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it cleanly for a weekly habit, and a screener needs no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing about any product, app or company reaches me; it just asks about my week.
screens.why6: It's one short question that can be answered in one breath, though the spoken form should end with 'Yes or no.' as the screener template does.

screens.why1: After asking if I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea before the questions about it makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and eye contact are words I use every day as someone who lip-reads and uses captions, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: Following people face to face while trying to keep eye contact instead of looking down at a phone is exactly my life.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options to pick.
screens.why5: It is an idea card shown on purpose, in plain words, and no company jargon or labels for people like me slip through.
screens.why6: Short separate sentences that say well aloud, though the second line repeats the first's live captions on glasses a little.

screens.why1: Right after the idea and the weekly-hearing-people question, asking how often this already goes wrong for me last month is an obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Miss" made me stop: did I miss a conversation by not going, or by sitting there and not following half of it, which is what actually happens to me?
screens.why3: I live this every week, but I don't keep count, and most conversations I half-follow rather than miss outright, so any number I gave would be a guess.
screens.why4: A box for the number, None for zero and I can't recall set apart covers every answer I could give without overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product or anyone's job titles comes through; it asks about my own conversations.
screens.why6: The question says well and the one escape comes last, but "A number of conversations last month" is a stray fragment when heard, and the None chip on screen is never said aloud.
screens.why7: One measure, the right period, a balanced open box and the one escape are all there, but the verb is the vague "miss" the card warns against, not the thing I actually see go: a conversation I couldn't follow.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations with hearing people could you not follow? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: After I've just said how many conversations I missed and seen the glasses idea, asking what they're worth makes sense, but it sits under 'What you do today' when it's really about a thing I don't have yet, so it comes a bit abruptly.
screens.why2: 'Up front' and 'a month' are how I already think about hearing aids and caption apps, and the dollar bands read straight off.
screens.why3: I pay for my own hearing gear and apps, so I know what I'd put down for something that let me follow a noisy table.
screens.why4: The bands don't overlap, they run from cheap to dear, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is a real answer of mine, and 'I can't say' sits apart as it should.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks, but '$599' looks like a shop sticker, so it reads as if someone has already priced these glasses.
screens.why6: Four short options at a time, then two, with the escape said once, so I could take it in on one hearing, and it reads just as well on screen.
screens.why7: Both ladders keep to price alone in dollars, up front and then a month, with an edge at what looks like the founder's low ($599, then $20), two bands below it plus 'wouldn't pay' against and three bands from it for, so the belief can be supported or refuted, and 'I can't say' is the one escape, apart.
screens.instead: Same question and bands, under a kicker like 'About the idea' rather than 'What you do today'.

screens.why1: Right after I gave a price, asking what would make it worth more follows naturally from what I just said.
screens.why2: The question itself is plain, but it reads my answer back as the band label, '$250 to under $599', where I'd just say 'about two hundred fifty to six hundred dollars'.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would make captions worth more to me: catching every word in a noisy restaurant, at the theatre, or at the doctor's, without fiddling with a phone.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was shown to me on the idea card on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or their words for people like me comes through.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but 'two hundred fifty to under five hundred ninety-nine dollars' is a mouthful to hear, and 'to under' is not how anyone talks.
screens.instead: You said about $250 to $600 for AirCaps. What would make it worth more to you?

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on AirCaps, it makes sense to ask whether I'd have needed anyone's OK the last time I paid for something like hearing aids or a captioning app.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself, though 'something like this' leaves me to decide it means hearing aids, a caption app or a listening gadget.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids and apps myself, and I know whether my partner, my audiologist or my insurance had a say.
screens.why4: The four run from me alone to someone else's decision and each one is different, and 'I can't say' sits apart as the way out.
screens.why5: Nothing about the founder's plan or their words for people leaks into this; it just asks about my last purchase.
screens.why6: Short question, four short options read as a list and one escape, though two of them start with 'someone else' and blur a little by ear.
screens.why7: With Nobody else tested, the screen has the four fixed answers in past form and in order, 'Someone else' in the second, and 'I can't say' as the one escape; only 'decided on my own' supports the belief, so it can be both supported and refuted.

screens.why1: After the price and who has to agree, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the obvious last question, though the kicker 'What you do today' doesn't really match a would-you question.
screens.why2: 'Order a pair with free returns' is how I'd say buying glasses I could send back, and I get it on one read.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd send off for captioning glasses I could return; it's my money and my conversations at stake.
screens.why4: A firm yes to the actual order, a soft yes, a soft no and a no cover every honest answer I'd give, with no overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing here goes beyond the idea card I was already shown; ordering glasses with free returns is my own way of putting it.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold after hearing them once, with no symbols or asides.
screens.why7: Every option is on the one measure of whether I'd take this step: the first yes names the founder's own step, 'Probably yes' is a softer yes to that same step, there are two answers for and two against so the belief could hold or fail, and there is no escape, as the card requires.
